articles.title: Ferran vs Pedri: los 'hermanos' íntimos se enfrentan por primera vez
articles.standfirst: El choque Champions entre PSG y Barcelona provocará el primer cara a cara de dos amigos inseparables que se conocieron en Valencia en octubre de 2019
articles.summary: El choque Champions entre PSG y Barcelona provocará el primer cara a cara de dos amigos inseparables que se conocieron en Valencia en octubre de 2019
articles.body: Son amigos, hermanos íntimos. Pedri y Ferran, Ferran y Pedri. Inseparables. Este martes, en París se verán las caras por vez primera en su carrera. Tantos años juntos, compartiendo vida, fútbol, programas de televisión, títulos, alegrías y momentos difíciles, pero nunca como rivales. El valenciano y el canario se pusieron cara hace ya muchos años en la playa de la Patacona de Alboraya (Valencia). Su agencia, Leaderbrok Sports los juntó cuando Pedri tenía 16 años y Ferran, con 19, ya triunfaba en el Valencia. Fue un encuentro en octubre de 2019, hace ya siete años, que cambió sus vidas. El destino y el mercado llevaron a uno al Barcelona y al otro al Manchester City el mismo verano de 2020 sin que les diera tiempo a medir sus fuerzas de delantero y centrocampista creador sobre el césped. Tampoco coincidieron en la Champions por lo que su head to head particular permanecía impoluto. En ese escenario Ferran fichó por el Barcelona y sus caminos se encontraron sobre el césped. Su amistad dio un salto y se hicieron 'familia'. En el Barça levantaron títulos y celebraron a lo grande. Siempre juntos, siempre ayudándose. Una complicidad que también se trasladó a la selección española y tampoco les fue mal. Una Eurocopa y un Mundial, casi nada. Más celebraciones y más complicidad. Una amistad que les llevó a estar muy juntos en los malos momentos como las críticas al delantero valenciano o las lesiones del canario. Este año los caminos deportivos, tras el mundial, se separaron de nuevo. Ferran firmó por el PSG y la pareja se rompió, solo en lo deportivo, obviamente. El sorteo de la Liga de campeones quiso que parisinos y catalanes (dos de los claros favoritos al título) se vayan a ver las caras en la tercera jornada de la fase liga de la Champions y allí, en el mejor partido que se puede ver ahora mismo en Europa se verán las caras por vez primera en su carrera, ya consolidada, Ferran y Pedri. El blaugrana sigue siendo una pieza clave en el Barça y su pareja con Rodri ya carbura en un centro del campo intocable, arrollador, la envidia de Europa. El de Foios, con la vitola del gol del mundial como bandera, ha llegado al PSG como un tornado. Goles en Liga, hat-trick en Champions en su debut y una sensación de que Luis Enrique sabía por quién apostaba. El martes habrá abrazo, no lo duden. Risas y seguro que alguna broma que otra. Sobre el campo competencia máxima y batalla por seguir en lo más alto de la fase Liga que ambos equipos, con el Aston Villa como invitado, dominan con puño de hierro.

articles.title: "Nos apoyamos en los principios de Luis Enrique para desarrollar a los jugadores"
articles.standfirst: El entrenador del filial del PSG explica para MARCA el método de trabajo con la cantera marcado por la filosofía y el estilo del asturiano
articles.summary: El entrenador del filial del PSG que afronta hoy la Youth League ante el Barça desgrana el método de trabajo de la cantera en consonancia con Luis
articles.body: El centro de entrenamiento del PSG es un hervidero de gente este lunes nublado en Poissy. Por aquí se palpa el trabajo y la tranquilidad, alejada de la tensión que se respira estos días en el centro de París. El equipo de la Youth League se mide en apenas 24 horas al Barça y luego en el Parque de los Príncipes lo hacen los dos equipos quizá más en forma de Europa. Luis Enrique dice que tienen muchas cosas en común, entre otras cosas el modelo de cantera y el de fijar una identidad muy marcada de juego desde el primer niño de la Fábrica hasta el último. París se ha convertido en una referencia en este sentido y más desde la llegada de Luis Enrique. MARCA ha estado hoy donde se cocina el talento en París, con los chavales que preparan el duelo ante el Barça en la Youth Ligue, y ha analizado con su entrenador Jean-François Vulliez, el método de trabajo con los cerca de 150 jugadores y jugadoras, 130 de ellos en la residencia. La Cité Educativa, que constituye una de las particularidades del modelo, permite acompañar a los jóvenes en su día a día a través del proyecto basado en tres pilares: deportivo, académico y socioeducativo. Una pasarela conecta los 16 campos, entre los del primer equipo y los de formación. La ciudad deportiva, que acaba de ser nombrada el mejor centro de formación de Francia por la Federación Francesa de Fútbol (FFF), cuenta con su propia metodología de formación, aunque se apoya en principios de juego comunes con el primer equipo de Luis Enrique para facilitar la progresión y la integración de los jóvenes. PREGUNTA: ¿Cómo es que llegaste a París y qué le sedujo del proyecto? RESPUESTA: Trabajé 13 años en Lyon. Fui director del centro de formación durante 6 años. Allí se terminó un ciclo, estuve un año en Dinamarca, pero en París buscaban un entrenador para los esfuerzos. Conocía a Yohan Cabaye (director del centro de formación). También conocía la calidad de los jugadores de París. Lo que me ha impresionado aquí es la calidad de las infraestructuras. Es increíble. El proceso de organización es muy profesional. Si necesitas cambiar una venda, tienes que llamar a alguien. Si necesitas una pizarra, tienes que llamar a alguien. Tienes un contexto de trabajo muy bueno. Y lo tercero es el número de personas de recursos humanos que tenemos a nuestro alrededor para ayudar a los jóvenes. Estas tres cosas son realmente impresionantes. P. ¿Y el espíritu de Luis Enrique está en toda la academia? R. Luis Enrique vino un par de meses antes de que yo. La dirección decidió, no lo impuso, seguir los principios de juego de Luis Enrique para favorecer el paso de los jóvenes del filial al primer equipo. Así que nos apoyamos en los principios de juego de Luis Enrique para desarrollar a los jugadores. Con una metodología de entrenamiento propia. No tenemos necesariamente los mismos jugadores pero, efectivamente, en los principios colectivos el objetivo es estar en las mismas estructuras de juego para facilitar el paso. Creo que es bueno tener una identidad común entre los jóvenes, al menos hasta el equipo filial. Y si además tienes una identidad común hasta los profesionales, es maravilloso. Y cuando tienes una estabilidad del entrenador, puedes crear un puente y un acercamiento entre todas las categorías. La fuerza de este proyecto es que hoy en día todos las equipos de formación, desde los sub 15 hasta mi equipo, juegan como quiere el entrenador. Eso permite a los jugadores desarrollarse en un modelo. Es una opción, aunque hay otras formas. P. ¿El modelo del Barça es una referencia? R. No hay un modelo en la formación que funcione y otro no. Hay varios. Los Países Bajos con el Ajax, el Barcelona, en Alemania o en Francia... Hay muchos modelos que funcionan. Pero aquí han decidido seguir los principios de Luis Enrique para desarrollar a los jugadores. Así que nosotros intentamos desarrollar a los jugadores en esos principios de juego, en las estructuras de juego que nos proponen. P. ¿Hay comunicación entre todos los entrenadores hasta el primer equipo? ¿Hay reuniones? R. Johan Cabaya y Mathieu Le Scornet (director técnico del centro de formación) suelen ser el enlace. Existe un seguimiento continuo de los jóvenes y una comunicación regular con el cuerpo técnico del primer equipo. Es precisamente uno de los puntos fuertes de nuestro proyecto. Luis Enrique y su staff ven muchos vídeos de nuestros partidos y recaban todos los datos de los jugadores. Luis Campos viene a vernos mucho. Y cuando hay un jugador que les interesa, piden más datos, más vídeos, montajes del vídeo de algún chaval para que, si necesitan, tengan un jugador que pueda subir con ellos. Así que son muy conscientes de la calidad de los jugadores que están aquí abajo. P. Hoy se miden a un rival con modelo de cantera, ¿es una referencia? R. Barcelona es un ejemplo, un modelo que es reconocido internacionalmente por las generaciones de jugadores que se han formado en el Barça o donde sea. Porque, como en Madrid, son clubes que forman muchos jugadores. Creo que Barcelona es reconocido por todas las generaciones de jugadores que han pasado o los que han hecho brillar al Barça. Es un modelo, por supuesto, que todos los clubes quieren seguir, pero París tiene su identidad de formación. Cada uno tiene la suya. P. ¿Cómo entrenador de cantera, cómo compagina la formación con el objetivo de ganar? R. Nuestro objetivo es poner el máximo de jugadores profesionales a la disposición de Luis Enrique. Y luego él hace la elección. En realidad, nuestro objetivo principal, nuestra razón de ser, es formarse. Pero la competición es parte de la formación. Es decir, ganar los partidos es parte de la formación. No se oponen a ganar y formarse. Creo que los dos están juntos. Y la fuerza del entrenador es no reaccionar y no estar atascado en el resultado. Damos todos los medios a los jugadores para ganar, pero si pierdes dándolo todo no es muy grave. Si es el resultado lo que guía tu pensamiento, no eres un formador. Puedes enfadarte si los jugadores no se esfuerzan. Ahí puedes enfadarte. P. Pero en el PSG hay otras dos patas muy claras, la educación y la formación. R. Tengo la sensación de que hay mucha formación a nivel humano con la residencia o con la escuela. Los educadores hablan con los chicos y están encima de todo y nosotros estamos en contacto con ellos. El jugador tiene un sistema para ayudar y acompañarlo. P. ¿Es muy exigente Luis Enrique? R. Es exigente, pero quiere ayudar al jugador a desarrollarse mentalmente. Cuando los jugadores suben, él también se toma su tiempo con ellos para explicarles sus expectativas. Es muy exigente, pero también es muy comunicativo con los jóvenes. El fútbol es muy exigente y hay muy poco sitio para todos. Para lograrlo, hay que trabajar, trabajar y trabajar... Y no es propio de París, a veces los jóvenes en la cultura francesa creen que será fácil porque son muy fuertes hasta los 16, 17, 18 o 19 años. Dominan sus partidos y ganan sus partidos. Es por eso que es bueno que haya encuentros más duros, que pierdan partidos, que estén en dificultad, que a veces hay que sufrir en el campo porque no lo han hecho. P. ¿Y ayuda que tengan una referencia en el primer equipo? R. Hay que mantener ese sueño el mayor tiempo posible. El año pasado 10 jugadores del centro jugaron con Luis Enrique. Este año, seis. Es importante que haya jugadores con el primer equipo. El último caso de 2009 es David Boly, que se entrena todos los días con el primer equipo. Y cuando puede viene a ver el vestuario, a ver nuestro partido, a saludar a sus compañeros. Por eso es importante que siempre haya un jugador que pueda estar arriba para crear esa línea social entre los jugadores que están conmigo y los jugadores que están en el primer equipo para hablar y mostrar que hay una puerta que puede abrirse. La puerta no está cerrada, pero hay que empujarla.

articles.title: James Maddison marks first Tottenham start in nearly 18 months with stunning goal in first Premier League win of season
articles.summary: Tottenham playmaker struck opener in 3-1 win over Coventry which moved side off foot of Premier League; the 29-year-old was making his first start following torrid long lay-off after suffering an ACL injury
articles.body:
The playmaker was influential in the 3-1 victory over Coventry in north London , opening the scoring with a curling strike from range to set Roberto De Zerbi's side on their way to a much-needed win which moves them off the foot of the table.

The 29-year-old, who has two years to run on his Spurs contract, first came back toward the end of last season after recovering from his ACL injury but has faced numerous setbacks that have delayed his full return until now.

"I have so much more to give for this club," Maddison told Sky Sports. "I'm 29 and I still have plenty of years left. I have self-belief and plenty of qualities that can help us in this league."

Spurs spent £334m on new signings in the summer after narrowly avoiding relegation from the Premier League but they have struggled to have the desired impact. Maddison wanted to show that he was the missing piece of the puzzle when given his chance.

Asked if he thought he could make this type of impact, Maddison added: "I hoped. I spoke to the gaffer [Roberto De Zerbi] about this week and feeling like it was the right moment for me to go back into the starting XI after a stop-start start to the season.

"I just wanted to play well and to show my qualities and what the team has missed in the last 18 months since my last start. The gaffer asked me to play and wanted to enjoy watching me from the side, so hopefully I did that. A goal like that is always nice."

Sky Sports pundit Jamie Carragher backed Maddison to have a big impact on Spurs' season when asked if he can be the glue that links the team together.

"I think he is seen as that type of player," said Carragher. "He's naturally one of those people in the game who is always laughing and joking, trying to lift people around the dressing room. I think he will have a big impact. He's captained the club in the past.

"Even though they've brought in a lot of attacking talent, he will still think no one's better than him because he's that type of character. He has that football arrogance that I like in players.

"It will be interesting to see where he fits in eventually because there are a lot of players at Tottenham in the attacking positions, especially with Kulusevski back."

Maddison found the top corner with a precise, curling effort that was teed up by Mohammed Kudus after just 14 minutes to give Spurs the start they needed after a dreadful start to the season on a tense night in north London.

"It was a joy to see [his goal]," said Sky Sports pundit Jamie Carragher on Monday Night Football. "He is one of the real characters in the game and you want him around Premier League football.

"That was just a great moment. When you're a player with an injury like that, there will be a fear: will you ever come back or will you be the same player? There is still a long way to go, but he still has a bit of magic in his boots!"

Maddison's last competitive start before the win over Coventry came in May 2025 when Ange Postecoglou was still in charge of Spurs, who have suffered desperately in the midfielder's absence, narrowly missing out on relegation last season.

Speaking about his goal, Maddison said: "They are the ones you dream of. Those dark days recovering from the ACL you dream of those moments and those goals. That is always the light at the end of the tunnel."

Maddison was not the only feel-good story for Spurs on Monday night. Dejan Kulusevski came off the bench to feature in a competitive game for the first time after 526 days out injured in what was an emotional return to the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.

"I felt really emotional and proud of Dejan Kulusevski today because I knew exactly that feeling he had stepping back onto the pitch after that amount of time out," said Maddison. "Those moments and those goals they make it all worth it."

"James Maddison was the star of the show and a big reason Spurs were able to secure the much-needed win. His goal speaks for itself.

"But the rest of his play also stood out, in a slightly more understated manner.

"He was dropping deep, finding pockets of space, threading passes for the runs of Dominic Solanke and threatening from the half spaces with his crossing ability.

"Spurs, after all their investment in the summer, looked disjointed and uninspiring across the opening six games.

"Maddison looks like the piece that could link the £300m pieces of this Spurs puzzle together. Whether that is through his own finishing or the ability to bring other players into the game.

"Keeping him fit and firing is now essential to the club building on this game."

articles.title: Egypt’s Hassan and Zico suspended over FIFA World Cup refereeing criticism
articles.summary: FIFA punishes Egypt’s head coach, forward and team manager for their comments after their World Cup loss to Argentina.
articles.body:
Egypt’s head coach Hossam Hassan and forward Mostafa Zico have paid the price for criticising the referee after their World Cup knockout loss to Argentina, with FIFA suspending the duo for three and five matches, respectively.

FIFA’s Disciplinary Committee handed down the sanctions, the Egyptian Football Association (EFA) said in a statement on Monday.

Hossam’s twin brother, Ibrahim, who is the national team’s manager, was also given a three-match suspension.

The EFA said it had submitted a request to the committee, seeking “the detailed reasons and justifications for the decisions”. The national football body is planning to appeal after assessing the legal aspects of the punishment.

The suspensions could rule Hossam and Ibrahim Hassan out of Egypt’s upcoming matches against Malawi in the next rounds of Africa Cup of Nations qualifying in November, as well as the first match of the March international window.

Egypt were knocked out in the round of 16 by Argentina, who came from 2-0 down to win the tense encounter in Atlanta, United States, on July 6.

The Pharaohs were left furious after a number of controversial calls went against them, including a disallowed goal early in the second half, and a member of their coaching staff was red-carded in the aftermath of the winning goal.

Hassan claimed his side was “cheated” out of a place in the quarterfinals after Argentina’s stunning late comeback.

“I do not want to put it nicely and talk about hard luck. We have been cheated unfairly today; we have suffered injustice,” Hassan said in an explosive post-match news conference.

Egypt had a Zico goal ruled out when they were leading 1-0 as the video assistant referee (VAR) intervened to spot a foul on Lisandro Martinez much earlier in the move.

Zico then put Egypt on the brink of a place in the last eight for the first time by doubling their lead.

However, the defending champions hit back as Cristian Romero reduced the arrears before Lionel Messi, who had a first-half penalty saved, smashed in the equaliser with his eighth goal of the tournament.

The controversy did not end there, though, as in the build-up to Argentina’s winner scored by Enzo Fernandez, Egypt believe they should have instead been awarded a penalty for a pull by Alexis Mac Allister on Hamdy Fathy.

“We haven’t seen respect or fair play. There has not been respect or fair play,” Hassan said.

“A penalty was ruled out; it was not even checked by VAR. A second goal was remarkably disallowed. There has not even been a VAR check when we have all seen the image of the [shirt] being pulled back.”

Zico had a goal ruled out for a foul in the build-up, before Egypt’s players appealed for a penalty near the end when the score was 2-2.

However, FIFA refereeing chief Pierluigi Collina defended the officiating in the match, saying such allegations could provoke threats against referees and their families.

articles.title: Viking’s Champions League adventure: Erik Nevland and Eirik Bjorno explain the Norwegian club’s rise from the depths
articles.summary: After stunning Bayern Munich in the Champions League, Norwegian club Viking are the talk of Europe. Adam Bate speaks to the club’s chief executive Eirik Bjorno and sporting director Erik Nevland, once of Manchester United, to find out more about their remarkable journey…
articles.body:
Champions League draw with Bayern Munich

Why the club means everything to Nevland

The low point of losing 5-0 in the second tier

Winning the title again after a 34-year wait

Why they do it differently with joint-coaches

Building something sustainable for the future

For Eirik Bjorno, Viking's chief executive, it was the first goal against Bayern Munich. "That was the moment," he tells Sky Sports . "You are preparing for wave after wave, maybe having a counter-attack or two, and then you score from the first corner."

Erik Nevland, the Norwegian club's sporting director, preferred the second. "You can always score early," he explains. "But that was something that we had never dreamed of. It was crazy. More than we could expect. It was just a night for the history books."

The third goal guaranteed that. Bayern had turned the game around with three goals of their own but Michael Olise was sent off and Viking seized the moment - their moment - to claim a draw on the night that Champions League football came to Stavanger.

"It was the biggest game in our club's history," says Bjorno. "The most important learning is that we can actually compete. We can actually cope with the tempo." Viking certainly did that, managing to upset the Bundesliga champions in more ways than one.

Max Eberl of the Bayern board was so ruffled by Zlatko Tripic's part in Michael Olise's red card that the executive made headlines by describing the Viking captain as a "scumbag" afterwards. "But he is our scumbag," says Nevland, laughing. "We love him."

To understand just why the 48-year-old Nevland is enjoying this moment so much, some context is needed. The former Norway international left Viking to join Manchester United as a teenager and played for the club in the Premier League, later featuring for Fulham.

But this is his club. There were four stints with Viking as a player but the love affair began much earlier. His mother even worked for the club. He has never known anything quite like this. "I have dreamed about this since I was five years old," Nevland explains.

"I played for the club from the age of seven and I never experienced this as a player. It is kind of a dream to win the league and to now represent Viking in the Champions League. This is my hometown club and it means everything. It is the proudest time of my life."

That pride also stems, in part, from the journey that this club has been on. Bjorno, like Nevland, remembers just how far Viking fell. Rock bottom arrived eight years ago in the second tier. "The low point was losing 5-0 against a team called Nest-Sotra," he recalls.

Bjorno seems to pause for comic effect. "That club does not exist anymore." It serves to underline the absurdity of it. This was June of 2018 and there were only 274 spectators there to see Viking go four behind before the end of the first half. This was their nadir.

"That was the absolute low point," confirms Bjorno. "It looked like we would not go up but we turned it around and got promoted by a point." Progress was steady thereafter, albeit with a wobble in 2022, before clinching the title for the first time in 34 years in 2025.

How? That is the obvious question. They say that acceptance is the first step on the road to recovery and Nevland's blunt assessment of that version of Viking would appear to attest to that theory. "We realised that we were bad. Something needed to change."

Bjorno, rather magnanimously, points to external factors. Norwegian football in general is enjoying an upturn in performance levels. "The federation started to make sure we were developing players." But that does not explain why it is Viking who have capitalised.

Nevland offers a hyper-local explanation. "We use our academy and have homegrown players. We also have people in leadership roles who love the club and want to do well, people who have a passion for the town and have been around the club for a long time."

Having people in key positions who really want to be at Viking is key, he believes. "This is the biggest job that they have had," Nevland explains. And that presence provides real continuity. "Players can come and go. But the culture that we have created is massive."

Viking's joint-coaches are an example not just of that continuity culture but also the club's willingness to do things differently. Bjarte Lunde Aarsheim played for the club for years, while fellow head coach Morten Jensen was also on the books as a teenager.

It is an unusual job-sharing arrangement but it works for Viking. "Regardless of what people think or what the natural thing to do is," says Bjorno, "we need to ask ourselves what the best decision is for Viking. We genuinely thought it would make us better."

Nevland actually sees it as a bonus that others are not taking this approach. "It was bold to do it that way. It was a gamble. But we were pretty sure we had to do something different to everyone else. It worked. Now, we almost cannot see another solution."

Sustaining this success will be difficult but Viking are doing well domestically too. They are battling with Bodo/Glimt to retain their Norwegian title for the first time in over 50 years. The two clubs are level on points with just seven games of the season remaining.

The danger in Europe's smaller leagues is that only one club accesses the Champions League money and the rest are simply left behind. With both teams in the biggest competition this season, there is the prospect of a different dynamic emerging in Norway.

"Financially, it is a different world," says Nevland. "It gives you a very solid foundation, more freedom and security. It also gives you the possibility to sign different kind of players." But the aim is to use the increased resources to build something longer term than that.

"We will definitely look at our facilities, our training ground, our stadium," adds Bjorno. "We want Viking to be strong 100 years from now. What decisions can we make now to ensure that the next generation will have the opportunity to keep developing the club?"

Nevland agrees. They will not get carried away. They want to focus on enjoying this moment. "The biggest danger in football is that you lose yourself very quickly because you are looking for success all the time. There are a lot of examples of that happening at bigger clubs."

Viking know who they are and what this means. "Everything," says Bjorno. "We spend all the time we have trying to make the club better. When you see so many kids with Viking jerseys around the city, this is what it is about. It is bigger than life in so many ways.

"We have been there when it was very dark so we know that it is a rollercoaster. We are just looking forward to the rest of this journey." With trips to Aston Villa, Atletico Madrid and Napoli still to come for Viking, there could be many more twists and turns ahead.

articles.title: Erik ten Hag interview: Man Utd’s broken ‘promises’, wanting Kane, Ronaldo tension, FA Cup glory
articles.summary: In the first of a two-part interview with The Athletic, former Man Utd boss Erik ten Hag unpacks his time at Old Trafford, including his unsuccessful push to bring in Harry Kane and his clashes with Cristiano Ronaldo
articles.body:
"I enjoyed every minute in Manchester United; I have such wonderful memories," says the former United manager. "It feels like I'm connected; I'm a fan. It's an amazing fanbase; they were always respectful to me.

"I really want United to win. I want them to be successful again. I want the club to be back where it once was."

That target feels a way off, with the mood around United turbulent once again. Ten Hag knows what it is like to be in the eye of the storm at the world's most talked-about club.

"The leadership, you need their competence, you need the right strategy," he says. "What is your identity? What are the work methods? You need the right structures and quality people. Then you need time."

That leads Ten Hag to talk about the man currently in the hot seat, Michael Carrick. "It is not the solution to dismiss him. 100 per cent not," he says. "Fans will demand this if results don't improve - it is coming out from the stomach, from the emotion. You have to make rational decisions. He showed good coaching abilities at Middlesbrough and last season. So let him do his process. I think he has a good staff."

The Athletic spent two evenings with Ten Hag in his hometown of Enschede, in the east of the Netherlands, to peel back the curtain on his two-and-a-half years managing United and to find out what his life is like now as technical director of FC Twente, his boyhood team.

In part one, Ten Hag gives fresh, fascinating insight into subjects including:

The broken "promises" that led to his sacking

Why he had to act on Cristiano Ronaldo, a player who "let the team down"

His desire to sign Harry Kane and Declan Rice, and pursuits of Brian Brobbey and Danny Welbeck

The "toxic culture" and what it was like managing players such as Marcus Rashford, Casemiro and Raphael Varane

Part two on Wednesday will address Ten Hag's offer to help United's data department, bringing through Kobbie Mainoo and Alejandro Garnacho, and why Sevilla was the turning point in his reign. You can also hear from Ten Hag on a special edition of our Talk of The Devils podcast later on Tuesday.

Ten Hag had looked set to lose his job on the eve of the 2024 FA Cup final against Manchester City at Wembley, as United's conversations with prospective successors, such as Thomas Tuchel and Roberto De Zerbi, had become public. But a 2-1 victory against Pep Guardiola's champions prompted a U-turn from the club's hierarchy. Ten Hag, after all, had claimed two trophies in two campaigns, following the League Cup 15 months earlier.

Two weeks later, the clause in his contract for an additional year was triggered after crunch talks during his holiday in Ibiza .

"I wouldn't go on with only one year left," says Ten Hag. "So I said, 'I need an extra year and we have to do it together'. They promised me loyalty, they promised me backing, they promised communication, that we get aligned. We spoke about the issues. But the promises, they didn't keep."

One of those 'promises', according to Ten Hag, was keeping Scott McTominay, who had scored 10 goals that campaign but ended up leaving United for Napoli later that summer for €30.5million (then £25.7m; $33.7m) as the club raised funds to buy Manuel Ugarte.

"That's why I got disappointed," Ten Hag adds. "In Ibiza, we agreed. I said, 'No selling Scott McTominay'. We would go aligned in the transfer window. I make an argument, a reason: we don't have scoring abilities. Scott brings scoring abilities and great mentality. He has United in all his veins. So when they bring up the subject, 'No'. And in the end they sold him. I got, of course, very embarrassed and disappointed."

Ten Hag did get Matthijs de Ligt and Noussair Mazraoui, two former Ajax players, but they had only two months together. United were 14th in the Premier League on 11 points from nine games when Ten Hag was dismissed on October 28, 2024, the day after his side lost 2-1 to West Ham United.

"I think it was quite weird to separate ways in that moment," he says, pointing out United were still in all the cup competitions. "All the data was showing we are good. OK, two poor games to Liverpool and Spurs (both 3-0 home defeats). We were starting the process. Let it progress; the gameplay is getting better."

Ten Hag feels he still had the dressing room onside. "Maybe they can say differently, but I see on the pitch, and every game they fought. Also, my last game, that was probably one of our best games, we should have won against West Ham. But I'm sure the process was already ongoing; there were already people - maybe even in the team - who knew what would happen the day after."

Three days before his sacking, Ten Hag detected something was amiss following United's 1-1 draw at Jose Mourinho's Fenerbahce in the Europa League - a competition he was convinced his team could win. United, led by Ruben Amorim, ended up losing the final that season 1-0 to Tottenham Hotspur in Bilbao.

"I can read situations; I see when people are not in Istanbul, all of a sudden something is going on," says Ten Hag. "But still, after that summer, where you get apologies for their behaviour, and that we would go to build, it's surprising.

"We targeted the Europa League. And I think when you choose a manager, and he proves the last two seasons, winning trophies, getting into finals, then I don't think it's good club management to change… I did watch the final, but everything was changed."

'Takeover process brought noise, uncertainty and disruptions'

Strength of mind is fundamental to Ten Hag. His bullishness invites the question of whether a manager at a club the scale of United needs an ego to avoid getting eaten up. "I don't have that ego, but I have the confidence," Ten Hag replies. "It's not about me; it is about the club. I can accept that new leadership is coming in and they want to appoint their own people, but just tell me."

Sir Jim Ratcliffe's investment in United was announced on December 24, 2023, bringing in Sir Dave Brailsford as a director. Omar Berrada was named as chief executive in January 2024, although he officially began the role in the July. Dan Ashworth had a period of gardening leave until that same month, so was not in Ibiza, before assuming his position as sporting director. Christopher Vivell also joined in July, initially as interim director of recruitment. Jason Wilcox was in the building from April, when he started work as technical director.

"The takeover process brought a lot of noise, uncertainty with the people, and disruptions," says Ten Hag. "So that was for the manager, for the coach, it was difficult to work, that's clear. It was very complicated."

Ten Hag had been interviewed by Ratcliffe and his brother, Bob, during Nice's hunt for a new head coach in 2021 and says he had a "good feeling" when their petrochemicals firm, INEOS, bought into United .

"But after the first meeting (at Carrington), he started talking about the structure in the football club, how the manager should be head coach," adds Ten Hag. "I said, 'OK, let's discuss, but my contract is different'. I never heard anything.

"Then every press conference (at United), they ask me if the structure should be changed. I always want to cooperate in a club - you can't do this on your own. You need to find a strategy about philosophy, game model, about team profile, individual profiles. That is what I was used to, but with them there was no communication."

It was a sign of things to come. As the stories swirled around United interviewing for his replacement in the build-up to facing Manchester City in the 2024 FA Cup final, Ten Hag was left in the dark. "There was a lot of speculation in the last two months," he says. "Every week articles came out about it. I can deal very well with it, but obviously we had our problems."

Ten Hag explains why he declined to go looking for answers. "I was thinking I'm the best manager for United, so it doesn't make sense to dive in," he says. "I was just focusing on my team. We had one chance to win a trophy, the FA Cup, and that's immense. So that's what we did.

"The celebrations on the pitch (at Wembley), let's say they were the best moment in my Manchester life."

Ten Hag did make his feelings known on some matters, however, and felt he was not supported in sanctions on several matters of player discipline, including with Jadon Sancho, Rashford and others.

"And so, they are continuing the toxic culture; they fuel it, they give the power to the players," he says. "Rashford is an amazing player, if his mindset is right. I always showed my trust in him, played him. But when you show these standards, sometimes you have to make corrections." United feel behaviours in the squad did improve, with Amorim supported by the hierarchy in moving players on. Rashford, who has been undergoing regular treatment to play through a hip injury in the early weeks of the season, enjoyed productive loans at Aston Villa and Barcelona following Ten Hag's departure and Carrick spoke in pre-season of the England international being "in great spirits".

Ten Hag felt he had to play bad cop to players to enforce the rules, yet at the same time he had to pick players he thought would win matches. It was a similar situation with Cristiano Ronaldo, a player Ten Hag inherited, the Portuguese having returned to Old Trafford for a second spell at the club in August 2021.

"He let the team down, and he let me down, because we planned with him," says Ten Hag. "I flew out to Portugal to speak with him about what I was aiming for before I came to United. Obviously, he's one of the best in football history. I respected him a lot. But at that time, as a manager, I had to make a rational decision and keep the players I admire in."

According to Ten Hag, Ronaldo pulled out of training sessions, did not get his heart rate raised to the required level when he did train, and only completed two of the three scheduled laps of the infamous run Ten Hag made his players do after they lost 4-0 at Brentford in August 2022 .

"I confronted him with this," says Ten Hag. "Many times I say, 'Ronnie, everyone wants to work for you to bring you in the right position, but if you can't bring yourself in the box, you can't score'. He was not capable to do this. It's the wrong idea to put this to me that I expected him to do the pressing, that he's exhausted. But he couldn't. He ran neither in possession nor out of possession. The reason was because he didn't prepare himself.

"Every top team has to embrace the top player, but the top player has to work for the team.

"He was telling the players, 'Save your legs at the training'. I understand it when you are top fit; you have sessions, you can save the legs. But first you have to train yourself to get into the right fitness levels."

The Athletic put Ten Hag's comments to Ronaldo's representative but had not received a reply at the time of publication.

Ronaldo's influence rubbed off on certain team-mates, Ten Hag believes. "Players have to act, they have a big responsibility. Football is, for some, not the highest priority. And United for some wasn't the highest priority."

Player power is back in vogue at United following Lisandro Martinez's extraordinary comments after the 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid last week. Martinez was disciplined internally for his comments, through a fine, and then made available for selection immediately.

Ten Hag declines to comment on the specifics of Martinez, but adds: "I can say I think that's what the Madrid connection brought in, that players are powerful and they want to decide. In my opinion it didn't suit the phase United was in. The leadership wanted attacking, dynamic football and these players wanted to play what fitted themselves."

By the "Madrid connection", Ten Hag means Casemiro, Varane, and Ronaldo, who won 14 Champions Leagues between them at Real Madrid under Zinedine Zidane and Carlo Ancelotti.

Casemiro came to United as the midfield strategist with "quarterback qualities", says Ten Hag. "Then of course it looked like he got demotivated. I don't know what they told him." The Athletic has previously reported Casemiro felt United would sign players to challenge for the title in summer 2023, having finished third in Ten Hag's first season.

Ten Hag tended to lean into the disciplinarian side of his character to try to bring order to a dysfunctional dressing room. Fred, the Brazilian midfielder, recently said Ten Hag was a great tactician but a poor man-manager. Ten Hag was sent a link to the interview.

"I'm not mad at Fred," he says, smiling. "You fight with your players when they are showing inefficient and unprepared standards. But it's always with respect. You want to push them, you want to get the best out of them."

Ten Hag was hired by former chief executive Richard Arnold and football director John Murtough based on the football of his Ajax team, who reached the Champions League semi-finals in 2019, beating Real Madrid 4-1 in the Bernabeu and Juventus 2-1 in Turin on the way.

"So our identity should be dynamic, attacking football, counter-press, and that is what Richard and John demanded me to do," he says. "Play possession in the opponent's half. Of course they want to win. Old Trafford is the Theatre of Dreams. They want adventure football. You then need the profiles.

"For me, you need the ball-playing centre-back and you need a ball-winning centre-half also able to play on a high line.

"I said for the first season, 'Centre-half, there's a problem, centre-midfield, there is a problem, and especially I need a strategist. Then we need goals'. And that was the biggest issue in all my three years: goals."

Barcelona's Frenkie de Jong was his first choice for midfield. United were in negotiations for several weeks, but the player declined to join.

"Everyone's thinking the manager is doing the negotiations, that I'm involved in financial issues, but I was never," says Ten Hag. "Of course, I did my best; I set up meetings with him, where it was Richard and John involved as well, to pursue him to come over. He could have been very important building the team, not only that year but for the future. But we didn't make it."

Ten Hag pressed for England midfielder Declan Rice instead. "The issue was that West Ham didn't want to let him go. I think we could have done more to test. We were on one page, they tried, but I don't know how the process went. The point is, at United you need outstanding players."

Rice, then 24, ended up moving to Arsenal in the summer of 2023 for a package worth £105m. He was instrumental in Mikel Arteta's side winning the Premier League for the first time in 22 years last season, often wearing the captain's armband, and has made the 30-man shortlist for the Ballon d'Or.

During that same window three years ago, Ten Hag had one name on his lips at centre-forward. "I said to them, 'I want only one player - and you know who'." He means Harry Kane, then aged 30. "I fought for it. I heard that he was very positive, but I never spoke with him about the issue. I don't know how the decision process went with John, Richard, the Glazers."

Ten Hag was told no. "They came to the conclusion. I don't have the insights in the financials."

Instead, Kane moved from Tottenham Hotspur to Bayern Munich in a €110m deal. The England captain has since scored 157 goals in 155 games for Bayern, twice lifting the Bundesliga, and is also nominated for this year's Ballon d'Or.

Ten Hag adds: "I think a club like United, you need these profiles to be successful. Personality, and they are mature, and they're accountable. We signed five, six players, young, high potentials. But they are not the finished product. They need guidance from good professionals, like Kane, Rice, and Bruno (Fernandes)."

Another who could have provided guidance the following year was Danny Welbeck, then 33 and at Brighton & Hove Albion. "For sure, we were in contact," says Ten Hag. "Not me, often Darren (Fletcher, then United technical director). And he was very interested."

The changing personnel of United's executive group meant the club never committed to a formal offer for Welbeck at that time.

Then there was Brian Brobbey, a former Ajax player Ten Hag wanted to support Ronaldo as a second striker in the summer of 2022.

"At first, not everyone was aligned," says Ten Hag. "Then we convinced him, but then we were late, and already he was in a different process."

Sunderland bought him in 2025 and he has scored 10 Premier League goals in 36 games.

Ten Hag's job now is to make sure FC Twente's squad is constructed using the right recruitment and all players are pulling in the same direction. It is not the scale of United, but Ten Hag still feels pressure to succeed.

"In the region it's very, very big," he says of the scrutiny he is under. "And this is a big club for the Netherlands. Not global, very clear, but there's always pressure as well. People are quite critical here. So, things have to work."

Ten Hag did get Matthijs de Ligt and Noussair Mazraoui, two former Ajax players, but they had only two months together. United were 14th in the Premier League on 11 points from nine games when Ten Hag was dismissed on October 28, 2024, the day after his side lost 2-1 to West Ham United.

"I think it was quite weird to separate ways in that moment," he says, pointing out United were still in all the cup competitions. "All the data was showing we are good. OK, two poor games to Liverpool and Spurs (both 3-0 home defeats). We were starting the process. Let it progress; the gameplay is getting better."

Ten Hag feels he still had the dressing room onside. "Maybe they can say differently, but I see on the pitch, and every game they fought. Also, my last game, that was probably one of our best games, we should have won against West Ham. But I'm sure the process was already ongoing; there were already people - maybe even in the team - who knew what would happen the day after."

Three days before his sacking, Ten Hag detected something was amiss following United's 1-1 draw at Jose Mourinho's Fenerbahce in the Europa League - a competition he was convinced his team could win. United, led by Ruben Amorim, ended up losing the final that season 1-0 to Tottenham Hotspur in Bilbao.

"I can read situations; I see when people are not in Istanbul, all of a sudden something is going on," says Ten Hag. "But still, after that summer, where you get apologies for their behaviour, and that we would go to build, it's surprising.

"We targeted the Europa League. And I think when you choose a manager, and he proves the last two seasons, winning trophies, getting into finals, then I don't think it's good club management to change… I did watch the final, but everything was changed."

'Takeover process brought noise, uncertainty and disruptions'

Strength of mind is fundamental to Ten Hag. His bullishness invites the question of whether a manager at a club the scale of United needs an ego to avoid getting eaten up. "I don't have that ego, but I have the confidence," Ten Hag replies. "It's not about me; it is about the club. I can accept that new leadership is coming in and they want to appoint their own people, but just tell me."

Sir Jim Ratcliffe's investment in United was announced on December 24, 2023, bringing in Sir Dave Brailsford as a director. Omar Berrada was named as chief executive in January 2024, although he officially began the role in the July. Dan Ashworth had a period of gardening leave until that same month, so was not in Ibiza, before assuming his position as sporting director. Christopher Vivell also joined in July, initially as interim director of recruitment. Jason Wilcox was in the building from April, when he started work as technical director.

"The takeover process brought a lot of noise, uncertainty with the people, and disruptions," says Ten Hag. "So that was for the manager, for the coach, it was difficult to work, that's clear. It was very complicated."

Ten Hag had been interviewed by Ratcliffe and his brother, Bob, during Nice's hunt for a new head coach in 2021 and says he had a "good feeling" when their petrochemicals firm, INEOS, bought into United .

"But after the first meeting (at Carrington), he started talking about the structure in the football club, how the manager should be head coach," adds Ten Hag. "I said, 'OK, let's discuss, but my contract is different'. I never heard anything.

"Then every press conference (at United), they ask me if the structure should be changed. I always want to cooperate in a club - you can't do this on your own. You need to find a strategy about philosophy, game model, about team profile, individual profiles. That is what I was used to, but with them there was no communication."

It was a sign of things to come. As the stories swirled around United interviewing for his replacement in the build-up to facing Manchester City in the 2024 FA Cup final, Ten Hag was left in the dark. "There was a lot of speculation in the last two months," he says. "Every week articles came out about it. I can deal very well with it, but obviously we had our problems."

Ten Hag explains why he declined to go looking for answers. "I was thinking I'm the best manager for United, so it doesn't make sense to dive in," he says. "I was just focusing on my team. We had one chance to win a trophy, the FA Cup, and that's immense. So that's what we did.

"The celebrations on the pitch (at Wembley), let's say they were the best moment in my Manchester life."

Ten Hag did make his feelings known on some matters, however, and felt he was not supported in sanctions on several matters of player discipline, including with Jadon Sancho, Rashford and others.

"And so, they are continuing the toxic culture; they fuel it, they give the power to the players," he says. "Rashford is an amazing player, if his mindset is right. I always showed my trust in him, played him. But when you show these standards, sometimes you have to make corrections." United feel behaviours in the squad did improve, with Amorim supported by the hierarchy in moving players on. Rashford, who has been undergoing regular treatment to play through a hip injury in the early weeks of the season, enjoyed productive loans at Aston Villa and Barcelona following Ten Hag's departure and Carrick spoke in pre-season of the England international being "in great spirits".

Ten Hag felt he had to play bad cop to players to enforce the rules, yet at the same time he had to pick players he thought would win matches. It was a similar situation with Cristiano Ronaldo, a player Ten Hag inherited, the Portuguese having returned to Old Trafford for a second spell at the club in August 2021.

"He let the team down, and he let me down, because we planned with him," says Ten Hag. "I flew out to Portugal to speak with him about what I was aiming for before I came to United. Obviously, he's one of the best in football history. I respected him a lot. But at that time, as a manager, I had to make a rational decision and keep the players I admire in."

According to Ten Hag, Ronaldo pulled out of training sessions, did not get his heart rate raised to the required level when he did train, and only completed two of the three scheduled laps of the infamous run Ten Hag made his players do after they lost 4-0 at Brentford in August 2022 .

"I confronted him with this," says Ten Hag. "Many times I say, 'Ronnie, everyone wants to work for you to bring you in the right position, but if you can't bring yourself in the box, you can't score'. He was not capable to do this. It's the wrong idea to put this to me that I expected him to do the pressing, that he's exhausted. But he couldn't. He ran neither in possession nor out of possession. The reason was because he didn't prepare himself.

"Every top team has to embrace the top player, but the top player has to work for the team.

"He was telling the players, 'Save your legs at the training'. I understand it when you are top fit; you have sessions, you can save the legs. But first you have to train yourself to get into the right fitness levels."

The Athletic put Ten Hag's comments to Ronaldo's representative but had not received a reply at the time of publication.

Ronaldo's influence rubbed off on certain team-mates, Ten Hag believes. "Players have to act, they have a big responsibility. Football is, for some, not the highest priority. And United for some wasn't the highest priority."

Player power is back in vogue at United following Lisandro Martinez's extraordinary comments after the 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid last week. Martinez was disciplined internally for his comments, through a fine, and then made available for selection immediately.

Ten Hag declines to comment on the specifics of Martinez, but adds: "I can say I think that's what the Madrid connection brought in, that players are powerful and they want to decide. In my opinion it didn't suit the phase United was in. The leadership wanted attacking, dynamic football and these players wanted to play what fitted themselves."

By the "Madrid connection", Ten Hag means Casemiro, Varane, and Ronaldo, who won 14 Champions Leagues between them at Real Madrid under Zinedine Zidane and Carlo Ancelotti.

Casemiro came to United as the midfield strategist with "quarterback qualities", says Ten Hag. "Then of course it looked like he got demotivated. I don't know what they told him." The Athletic has previously reported Casemiro felt United would sign players to challenge for the title in summer 2023, having finished third in Ten Hag's first season.

Ten Hag tended to lean into the disciplinarian side of his character to try to bring order to a dysfunctional dressing room. Fred, the Brazilian midfielder, recently said Ten Hag was a great tactician but a poor man-manager. Ten Hag was sent a link to the interview.

"I'm not mad at Fred," he says, smiling. "You fight with your players when they are showing inefficient and unprepared standards. But it's always with respect. You want to push them, you want to get the best out of them."

Ten Hag was hired by former chief executive Richard Arnold and football director John Murtough based on the football of his Ajax team, who reached the Champions League semi-finals in 2019, beating Real Madrid 4-1 in the Bernabeu and Juventus 2-1 in Turin on the way.

"So our identity should be dynamic, attacking football, counter-press, and that is what Richard and John demanded me to do," he says. "Play possession in the opponent's half. Of course they want to win. Old Trafford is the Theatre of Dreams. They want adventure football. You then need the profiles.

"For me, you need the ball-playing centre-back and you need a ball-winning centre-half also able to play on a high line.

"I said for the first season, 'Centre-half, there's a problem, centre-midfield, there is a problem, and especially I need a strategist. Then we need goals'. And that was the biggest issue in all my three years: goals."

Barcelona's Frenkie de Jong was his first choice for midfield. United were in negotiations for several weeks, but the player declined to join.

"Everyone's thinking the manager is doing the negotiations, that I'm involved in financial issues, but I was never," says Ten Hag. "Of course, I did my best; I set up meetings with him, where it was Richard and John involved as well, to pursue him to come over. He could have been very important building the team, not only that year but for the future. But we didn't make it."

Ten Hag pressed for England midfielder Declan Rice instead. "The issue was that West Ham didn't want to let him go. I think we could have done more to test. We were on one page, they tried, but I don't know how the process went. The point is, at United you need outstanding players."

Rice, then 24, ended up moving to Arsenal in the summer of 2023 for a package worth £105m. He was instrumental in Mikel Arteta's side winning the Premier League for the first time in 22 years last season, often wearing the captain's armband, and has made the 30-man shortlist for the Ballon d'Or.

During that same window three years ago, Ten Hag had one name on his lips at centre-forward. "I said to them, 'I want only one player - and you know who'." He means Harry Kane, then aged 30. "I fought for it. I heard that he was very positive, but I never spoke with him about the issue. I don't know how the decision process went with John, Richard, the Glazers."

Ten Hag was told no. "They came to the conclusion. I don't have the insights in the financials."

Instead, Kane moved from Tottenham Hotspur to Bayern Munich in a €110m deal. The England captain has since scored 157 goals in 155 games for Bayern, twice lifting the Bundesliga, and is also nominated for this year's Ballon d'Or.

Ten Hag adds: "I think a club like United, you need these profiles to be successful. Personality, and they are mature, and they're accountable. We signed five, six players, young, high potentials. But they are not the finished product. They need guidance from good professionals, like Kane, Rice, and Bruno (Fernandes)."

Another who could have provided guidance the following year was Danny Welbeck, then 33 and at Brighton & Hove Albion. "For sure, we were in contact," says Ten Hag. "Not me, often Darren (Fletcher, then United technical director). And he was very interested."

The changing personnel of United's executive group meant the club never committed to a formal offer for Welbeck at that time.

Then there was Brian Brobbey, a former Ajax player Ten Hag wanted to support Ronaldo as a second striker in the summer of 2022.

"At first, not everyone was aligned," says Ten Hag. "Then we convinced him, but then we were late, and already he was in a different process."

Sunderland bought him in 2025 and he has scored 10 Premier League goals in 36 games.

Ten Hag's job now is to make sure FC Twente's squad is constructed using the right recruitment and all players are pulling in the same direction. It is not the scale of United, but Ten Hag still feels pressure to succeed.

"In the region it's very, very big," he says of the scrutiny he is under. "And this is a big club for the Netherlands. Not global, very clear, but there's always pressure as well. People are quite critical here. So, things have to work."

articles.title: SPFL invites bids for Scottish Premiership TV rights from 2029-30
articles.summary: The SPFL expects "strong interest" after inviting broadcasters to bid for the UK rights to show Scottish Premiership matches from the 2029-30 campaign.
articles.body:
The SPFL expects "strong interest" after inviting broadcasters to bid for the UK rights to show Scottish Premiership matches from the 2029-30 campaign.

The league's current five-year, £150m agreement with Sky Sports , which allows the broadcaster to show up to 60 games a season, began last term and will end at the conclusion of the 2028-29 campaign.

Premier Sports can also show up to 22 Scottish top-flight fixtures per season, but the SPFL says it is "flexible about the number of games that it shows live in future".

"Securing strong broadcast partnerships is an essential element in maintaining a balanced and sustainable income mix for the SPFL and its clubs," said SPFL chief executive Neil Doncaster.

"We anticipate strong interest from broadcasters in what is widely recognised as one of Europe's most exciting national league competitions."

The SPFL confirmed that a separate contract with Premier Sports covering broadcast and sponsorship rights for the Scottish League Cup is in place until at least the end of the 2030-31 season and will not be affected by this announcement.

articles.title: Pleno del Betis como local contra rivales neerlandeses
articles.standfirst: Los verdiblancos reciben mañanan al Feyenoord en su tercer partido de la Champions League
articles.summary: Los verdiblancos reciben mañanan al Feyenoord en su tercer partido de la Champions League
articles.body: El Betis recibe mañana (21.00 horas) al Feyenoord en La Cartuja en la tercera jornada de la liguilla de la Champions League. Los de Manuel Pellegrini han hecho pleno hasta la fecha en su regreso a la máxima competición continental con dos remontadas ante el Lille a domicilio (2-3) y en casa frente al Porto (3-2). Los verdiblancos vuelven a jugar frente a su afición y, con los números —o, más bien, los marcadores— a su favor, las estadísticas favorecen a los andaluces ante equipos neerlandeses cuando juegan como locales. El ejemplo más cerca fue la visita, precisamente del Feyenoord, a La Cartuja el pasado 29 de enero, en el cierre de la liguilla de la Liga Europa. Los goles de Antony y Abde -y el visitante Tengstedt- le dieron la victoria al equipo de Manuel Pellegrini. Anteriormente, en noviembre y en la misma competición, el Utrecht perdió 2-1 ante los verdiblancos, gracias a los goles de Cucho Hernández y Abde, descontados en la segunda parte por el gallego Miguel Gutiérrez. En la segunda eliminatoria de la Copa de la UEFA de la temporada 1995/96, con Lorenzo Serra Ferrer entonces en el banquillo, el Betis eliminó al Willem II después de empatar a uno en Tilburgo y gracias al 3-0 que le endosó en Benito Villamarín, donde marcaron Finidi, Benjamín y Fernando. La última referencia la encontramos diez cursos más tarde, en la ida de los dieciseisavos de la misma competición. 2-0 frente al AZ Alkmaar en la capital hispalense. Vieron puerta los brasileños Diego Tardelli y Robert da Pinho, y también fue apeado por los verdiblancos, que decantaron la eliminatoria en la prórroga disputada en los Países Bajos.

articles.title: Los árbitros, esos seres de luz
articles.standfirst: Nacional IV - Por Tomás Campos
articles.summary: Nacional IV - Por Tomás Campos
articles.body: Hay pruebas fehacientes de políticos corruptos. Ejemplos manifiestos de curas que han abusado de menores, hasta el punto de avergonzar a la Iglesia en boca del difunto Papa Francisco. Y hay incluso padres y madres que asesinan a sus hijos, cometiendo un crimen especialmente abominable. Nadie pone en duda estas afirmaciones porque las pruebas son irrefutables, alcanzando de hecho a casi todos los estamentos y grupos sociales. Eso sí, sigue existiendo un gremio ajeno a las miserias humanas. Un colectivo que levita por encima del resto impartiendo justicia en un mundo que no les merece. Hablamos lógicamente de los árbitros, y muy especialmente de los españoles. Seres de luz que sufren el acaso impenitente de la turba, incapaz de comprender que los errores forman parte de la vida y, por supuesto, del fútbol. Porque hay que ser muy torticero para pensar que un árbitro se equivoca (o inhibe) a propósito y se ve condicionado a la hora de pitar un partido, sobre todo si Real Madrid o Barcelona están en liza. Habrá quien, preso del rencor, argumente que no es lo mismo cobrar hasta 400.000 euros al año (en el caso de los internacionales) que 100.000 en Segunda y que se vive más tranquilo equivocándose a favor de los poderosos porque la presión mediática puede hasta afectar a tu entorno familiar. Y hay incluso quien piensa que arbitran de distinta forma un partido con equipos menores de la zona baja de la tabla que un duelo entre grandes. Que las tarjetas vuelan con mayor facilidad y de forma más caprichosa en el primero de los casos, hablando a los jugadores con menor respeto que a nuestros ilustres campeones mundiales, por poner un ejemplo. La locura es tal que hay quien ha llegado a cuestionar la honradez de estos seres bendecidos por la diosa Temis porque un vicepresidente del Comité Técnico de Árbitros (CTA) aceptó dinero del Barcelona durante casi dos décadas. El argumento, pueril a todas luces, es que el tal José María Enríquez Negreira -que así se llama el buen hombre que se embolsó 8,4 millones de euros- decidía en gran medida qué árbitros perdían la categoría o subían a Primera. Ni que decir tiene que ningún árbitro ha abierto la boca en este caso, porque hacerlo sería rebajarse al lodazal moral que invade al resto de los mortales. Son tan, pero tan celestiales nuestros colegiados que han despertado la envidia de sus congéneres en el resto del mundo, que han decidido relegarles a un papel muy secundario en competiciones internacionales como la Copa del Mundo o la Liga de Campeones. Los malpensados defienden que es en represalia por el caso Negreira pero qué sabrán ellos. Y así seguimos, dudando de lo único bueno, puro y sensato que queda en el fútbol. Porque habrá quien piense que no hay inocencia mayor que la de un niño pero eso es porque no tiene la suerte de conocer a un árbitro español de Primera división...

articles.title: Luís Castro: "Podríamos pedir a la liga hacer una liga con los últimos quince minutos de partido, pero seguro que no nos escucharían"
articles.standfirst: El entrenador portugués del Levante ha confirmado la posibilidad del retorno de Etta Eyong a la convocatoria tras superar su lesión
articles.summary: El entrenador portugués del Levante ha confirmado la posibilidad del retorno de Etta Eyong a la convocatoria tras superar su lesión
articles.body: El entrenador portugués del Levante ha confirmado la posibilidad del retorno de Etta Eyong a la convocatoria tras superar su lesión Partido que condiciona "No queríamos tantos partidos cerca, pero es lo que hay. Tenemos que mirar como otro partido. Vamos a jugar contra un equipo muy bueno, un club histórico y que tiene individualidades de muy buen nivel. Es un partido atrasado y si ganamos puntos, solo los ganamos nosotros" Enfermería "Hugo Sotelo ya está entrenando y Etta, que no estaba entrenando al 100%, ya lo está haciendo y vamos a ver sus sensaciones. Etta es posible que esté convocado. Hay molestias en algunos jugadores, por aquello de los partidos, pero vamos a ver cómo se encuentran después del entrenamiento. Hablaré con el doctor cuando salga de aquí. Hay más de uno, pero son jugadores que, después del parón hemos jugado dos partidos con intensidad muy alta y han sido partidos muy disputados hasta el final. Es una situación normal" Juego del equipo fuera de casa "Normalmente la valoración del equipo va unida al resultado. Dentro de nuestra planificación, nosotros también lo hacemos después del partido. En el último encuentro, contra el Dépor, presionamos en el área contraria y para nosotros lo que nos ha faltado es que nos ha faltado explosión en el área contraria. Hemos corrido riesgos para ganar. Hemos peleado hasta el final. Si estamos 1 a 1, el equipo en bloque bajo, ahí puedo comprender, pero el equipo peleó para ganar. Los partidos como visitante, sin contar ante el Espanyol, podríamos haber perdido o ganado, pero hemos peleado hasta el final" Jugadores que suman a la causa "Requena y Ratkov, se están acercando muchos y en los entrenamientos hay otros que se han acercado mucho. Ahora, cuando tengan minutos, tienen que demostrar lo que hacen en los entrenamientos. Están trabajando todos muy bien. Están todos más cerca de lo que creemos. Hugo Sotelo estaba muy bien y luego se lesiona, pero estaba muy cerca de lo que queríamos. Poco a poco vamos ganando jugadores" Rival, Athletic "Nico normalmente jugó contra nosotros y lo hace normalmente. No lo sé si jugará mañana. Hace mucho tiempo que el Athletic no pierde un partido. Tiene mucha calidad individual y en todas las posiciones tiene algunos que son campeones del mundo y han jugado de titular toda la temporada. Tienen nivel de los mejores jugadores del mundo. En cualquier momento te puede hacer mucho daño y tenemos que estar muy concentrado. Si están bien, te pueden hacer daño en todos los lados. No han cambiado mucho del año pasado y los posicionamientos y el sistema es prácticamente el mismo" El Levante de la Primera y Segunda mitad, completamente diferente "Yo saco siempre conclusiones positivas. El partido tiene noventa minutos y tenemos que estar bien durante todo el partido. Podríamos pedir a la liga hacer una liga de los últimos quince, pero seguro que no nos escucharían. Hay momentos que podemos mejorar, como la primera mitad del último partido que no sufrimos, y poco a poco mejoraremos" Marc Santos "Es un jugador de la primera plantilla y tiene nivel para jugar en Primera División. Está claro que, por su edad, tiene menos minutos y tienen que darle competición. cuando juega con el filial es importante para nosotros. Tenemos que saber que hay un viaje y cuando lo necesitamos con nosotros, jugará. Juega bien de 3,11 y de 8, es capaz de jugar en todas las posiciones muy bien" Competencia en el lateral derecho "Los dos están bien. A Toljan todo el mundo lo conoce y Nacho la tendrá. El año pasado, no tuvimos problemas en meter a Nacho en el terreno de juego porque sabíamos que iba a competir. Jugó contra el Valencia y Mallorca y nos daba garantías de que tenía nivel. No estoy mirando los minutos de juego, pero los dos están cerca y tienen perfiles diferentes y nos puede aportar cosas importantes. Son dos jugadores que trabajan siempre al 100% y son profesionales muy buenos" Oriol Rey y su competencia "Oriol está mejor que cuando llegué. Ofensivamente es muy bueno y defensivamente ha mejorado mucho. Es un jugador muy inteligente y, como a nosotros nos gusta jugar, él está bienvenido. Con partidos muy cerca, como tenemos ahora, era difícil que jugará todos los minutos de los partidos. Axel está muy cerca y está cerca de lo que queremos"

articles.title: Report Card Grades for Top 20 College Football QBs After Week 7
articles.summary: Every Tuesday morning throughout the 2026 college football season, we will be grading the performance of the top 20 quarterbacks in the nation, then re-ranking a new top 20 for next week's report card assignment.
articles.body:
Every Tuesday morning throughout the 2026 college football season, we will be grading the performance of the top 20 quarterbacks in the nation, then re-ranking a new top 20 for next week's report card assignment.

Included are each player's numbers through the air and on the ground, their game's outcome, and the quality of their opponent. A 1-5 star system was used to highlight the quality of the opponent, using the most recent version of The Athletic's ranking of all 138 FBS teams, with stars awarded as follows:

5 stars: No. 1-10 in the rankings 4 stars: No. 11-40 in the rankings 3 stars: No. 41-70 in the rankings 2 stars: No. 71-100 in the rankings 1 star: No. 101-138 in the rankings or an FCS opponent

Each quarterback's performance was given a grade of A, B, C, D or F. Those grades were factored into the reordering of the rankings for the following week.

Week 7 Passing Stats: 21-of-28, 158 yards, 2 TD, 0 INT Week 7 Rushing Stats: 7 carries, 4 yards Week 7 Quality of Opponent: ★★★★ (Oklahoma) Week 7 Outcome: Win (21-13)

Kentucky is up to No. 12 in the latest AP poll thanks to a 6-1 start, which is a far cry from where most predicted them to be after they were picked to finish 14th in the SEC preseason media poll.

Notre Dame transfer Kenny Minchey has been a big reason for their unexpected success, completing 68.4 percent of his passes for 1,552 yards and 13 touchdowns while throwing only one interception. The former 4-star recruit led a fourth-quarter touchdown drive to give Kentucky a 14-13 lead on Saturday. The defense iced it with a pick-six.

Week 7 Passing Stats: 23-of-36, 224 yards, 1 TD, 1 INT Week 7 Rushing Stats: 13 carries, 45 yards, 2 TD Week 7 Receiving Stats: 1 catch, 15 yards, 1 TD Week 7 Quality of Opponent: ★★★★★ (Notre Dame) Week 7 Outcome: Win (28-24)

With a passing touchdown, two rushing touchdowns and even a receiving touchdown, Bear Bachmeier did it all in arguably the biggest game of his career, leading BYU to a victory over Notre Dame.

That win vaulted the Cougars to No. 2 in the latest AP poll. Bachmeier has made a significant leap up the Heisman Trophy odds board. His interception came in the fourth quarter with BYU trailing 24-21, but the defense forced a three-and-out. Bachmeier responded with a 10-play, 55-yard drive to take the lead for good.
